assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice concept, and its realization in strontium and ytterbium clocks, removed the usual trade-off between atom number and Doppler or recoil shifts. Lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level are among the most precise measurements ever made. They test fundamental constants and relativistic time dilation over centimetre height differences, and they point toward a redefinition of the second. A clean idea gave a qualitatively new capability, and I judge it by precision and by theory-experiment agreement, which I value highly.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first lattice clocks. Ye's group then took strontium lattice clocks to record accuracy and stability. The two-person credit is clean and I see no serious dispute, though other groups (for example SYRTE and PTB/NIST) contributed to the clock development and I rely on my own recollection of the history.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed the early results, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree. Recognition looks timely, as the natural continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
How to weigh the original concept against the later record-setting implementation; I have not independently verified the priority history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal showed how to implement quantum logic gates with laser-cooled ions in a linear trap, turning abstract quantum computation into a concrete physical programme. Trapped-ion experiments (very high gate fidelities, many-ion entanglement, quantum simulation) provide some of the clearest controlled quantum many-body systems. The physics is fundamental and sits in my own field.
assessment.attribution: The proposal is clearly Cirac and Zoller. Blatt's group made the first realization of the Cirac-Zoller gate and led many-ion entanglement. Wineland (2012 laureate) and groups such as Monroe's made closely related early gate demonstrations, so Blatt as third name is defensible but not obvious.
assessment.maturity: The approach has been replicated by several independent groups and remains a leading platform. Earlier prizes (2012, 2022) touched on related physics, so timing is plausible but the area may be crowded.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 recognition of ion control and the 2022 entanglement prize.
Whether the third place is better held by Blatt or by an experimentalist from the NIST tradition; the supplied names do not include the alternative.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters. The superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, quantum gas microscopes and quantum simulation of magnetism and transport reveal quantum many-body physics in a controlled setting. The theoretical proposals for lattice Hubbard models gave the programme its direction. These are fundamental questions about interacting quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Five names are credited. A three-person configuration could use Zoller for theory, Bloch for the programme and Greiner for the Mott-insulator and gas-microscope experiments. Dalibard and Cirac are important but I would leave them off to keep a clean claim; this is the part I am least sure about, and key figures such as Jaksch and Hansch are not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Foundational results are widely reproduced and the field is mature. Some of the larger promises of quantum simulation are not yet demonstrated, though the established demonstrations are strong.
uncertainties: Large overlap with the Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion candidate; two prizes for the same theory pair would be unwise.
Credit gap: the original Mott-insulator experiment involved a larger group than the names supplied.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry gives inertial and gravitational sensors of extreme sensitivity, with precision measurements of the fine-structure constant, G and local gravity and tests of the equivalence principle. The idea that atoms act as waves with phase set by laser pulses is conceptually clean and speaks to the quantum-classical boundary.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of atom-light interferometry, Pritchard's early atom interferometers with gratings and Kasevich's light-pulse interferometry are each important, but credit is plainly shared among more people (for example Chu, Mlynek, Ketterle and others). A three-name configuration leaves out some groups, so a fair allocation is hard.
assessment.maturity: Atom interferometers are used in many laboratories and are nearing field applications, though the largest fundamental tests are still being improved. The Chu share of the 1997 laser-cooling prize may weigh in the committee's mind.
uncertainties: Impact on fundamental physics is so far more instrumental than a decisive new finding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED achieved strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon and is the basis of most superconducting quantum processors, dispersive readout and quantum-limited amplification. The transfer of cavity QED from atoms to chips is elegant and high in impact. I recognise it as the solid-state descendant of cavity-QED experiments in atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are all central to the 2004 proposal and demonstration. I would take Blais as theory lead with Wallraff and Schoelkopf for the experiments, but the choice between Girvin and Blais is a close call and I am not confident which better reflects historical leadership.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce the central results and the field is mature. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, a closely related area, so the committee may consider it too soon.
uncertainties: Timeliness after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Whether the committee wishes to recognise the physics (cavity QED on a chip) or the platform's technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that the phase of a quantum state carries physical information beyond local fields, and they underpin topological phases, polarization optics, molecular conical intersections and quantum computing. This is a clear case of an unexpected, fundamental insight into how quantum mechanics works.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm predicted the effect in 1959. Bohm is deceased and a prize cannot go to him, and Ehrenberg and Siday had an earlier version. Berry's 1984 phase had precursors (Pancharatnam) and was extended by Aharonov and Anandan and by Simon. Aharonov and Berry are a reasonable pair but the credit story is delicate, and I rely on recollection for these priority details.
assessment.maturity: Experiments confirm both effects strongly. Recognition is arguably late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Bohm's death and the priority of Ehrenberg and Siday and of Pancharatnam.
Whether Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase are one discovery or two.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state, entangling them with light and with qubits, and observing quantum behaviour in objects containing vast numbers of atoms address the question I care most about, namely where the boundary between quantum and classical lies. Optomechanical techniques have also produced useful sensors, including quantum-noise reduction in gravitational-wave detectors.
assessment.attribution: Cleland's group demonstrated ground-state cooling of a mechanical resonator coupled to a qubit; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer made the optical-regime milestones. Credit is spread across more than three people, and others (for example Painter, Teufel, Harris, Schwab) are not among the credited names, so a fair split is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The field is younger than my higher-ranked entries. The milestone experiments are reproduced on several platforms, but the broader fundamental payoff (testing quantum mechanics at larger masses) is still developing, so recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Many equally deserving contributors outside the supplied names.
Overlap in theme with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling molecules to ultracold temperatures and controlling their states enables precision tests (such as electron electric dipole moment searches), ultracold chemistry and dipolar quantum gases. It continues the atomic-cooling tradition and the EDM limits probe physics beyond the Standard Model.
assessment.attribution: Buffer-gas cooling, direct laser cooling with EDM measurements, and work on molecules in traps and ultracold chemistry are each important, but the field has many contributors (for example Meijer, Jin, Ni, Cornish, Hinds). The three names are a defensible subset but not clearly the decisive trio.
assessment.maturity: Direct laser cooling and ultracold molecule assembly have been reproduced by several groups, but the largest payoffs (a nonzero EDM or a clear quantum-simulation result) are not yet in hand. I regard this as premature relative to my higher-ranked entries.
uncertainties: Ye also appears in the lattice-clock candidate.
The strongest scientific result so far is a null EDM bound.
